findings.text: The opening paragraph says what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves. A newcomer can explain the project after this one paragraph.
findings.source: header, first lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why the rest of it is about a different project, firstmate. Without this, a visitor to Athena's site would be confused to find a study of another tool. The framing works.
findings.source: header, second lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it..."

findings.text: The page shows itself as Athena's demonstration, but it never shows the features the opening promises: which models wrote and checked this study, what it cost, or the verdict. A newcomer sees the claim tracing but not the accountability record that is meant to set Athena apart.
findings.source: header lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost" (no cost, model or verdict appears anywhere else on the page)

findings.text: The next steps are concrete, and the top of the page links to them. The list gives prerequisites, the install command and a first command to try. That answers 'what do I do next'.
findings.source: Next steps: "Get the code: git clone ...", "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh", "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Athena is described as written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not mention a Rust toolchain or say whether setup.sh installs one. A newcomer may wonder whether the install will work.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link is aimed at the repository owner, but it sits in the newcomer's first screen with no explanation. A first-time reader cannot tell whether 'your decision' means them.
findings.source: header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The 'Start here' section gives a clear plain-language summary of firstmate and walks one task from start to finish. It defines terms before using them. A newcomer can follow it.
findings.source: Start here: "What firstmate is" and "One piece of work, start to finish"

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state machine, design cards, a 40-entry glossary and 45 claims. Several definitions are repeated ('Words used first' and the Glossary define captain, yolo, green, red and in scope twice). A newcomer will likely stop reading after 'Start here'. The detail does support the traceability point, though.
findings.source: Transitions (t1–t12), Why it is built this way, Glossary, Claims and sources (c1–c45)

findings.text: The page states openly what it does not know and that nothing was run. This supports its message about accountability.
findings.source: Glossary, in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."; Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"

findings.text: This section uses internal repository terms that mean nothing to a newcomer, since the page does not link to that folder.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
